newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UNICEF says reform must not mean loss of identity.
newsitem.headline: UNICEF says reform must not mean loss of identity.

text.p: The U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) must not lose its independent identity in any consolidation of agencies resulting from U.N. reform, its executive director, Carol Bellamy, said on Monday.

"It is not an overstatement to say that our progress in ensuring the development and well-being of children and women, and in building support for the Convention on the Rights of the Child, will continue to depend on UNICEF's independent voice and identity," she said.
Addressing the opening of the 1997 annual session of the UNICEF executive board, Bellamy stressed she was deeply committed to the reform process both within UNICEF and in the U.N. system as a whole.

"It is self-evident that no other United Nations agency speaks directly for children, day in and day out, globally and locally," she said. "If that voice is muted or even stilled, there is a real and present danger that children will come a lesser priority.

Referring to a reform package that Secretary-General Kofi Annan is expected to unveil in mid-July, she said the options included alternatives as far-reaching as the creation of a new humanitarian affairs agency into which U.N. bodies handling emergencies -- including UNICEF -- would be consolidated.

Under that scenario, she said, the office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) would effectively become the U.N. humanitarian organisation, with wider powers than it currently possessed. UNHCR would also encompass the New York-based Department of Humanitarian Affairs, diplomats said.

Another reform plan under consideration places UNICEF into a cluster of development agencies in New York that would be comprised of the U.N. Development Programme and the U.N. Population Fund, diplomats said. The object, is to share administration and overhead, especially in the field.

Bellamy, a former director of the United States Peace Corps and a former president of the New York City Council, said UNICEF must have continued access to the senior political leadership of the countries in which it operated.
"UNICEF's voice must remain strong and identifiable in the social and economic dialogues and in the planning process."

"We believe that within any collaborative and coordinated framework, it remains vital that we retain our capacity and authority to speak directly for children everywhere, to develop and implement discrete country programmes under your guidance, and to carry out our own fund-raising," she told the UNICEF board.
